```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)

# Colours (colour-blind safe, no red)
col_base <- "grey80"   # grey
col_high <- "#E69F00"   # orange (highlight)

```


```{r data}
# Data: barley.csv (same folder as this file)
barley <- read_csv("Data/barley.csv") |>
  mutate(year = factor(year))
```



```{r}
# Sites ordered by overall mean yield, so rows read bottom -> top
site_order <- barley |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(m = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(m) |>
  pull(site)

barley <- barley |>
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_order),
         is_morris = site == "Morris")

# Cleveland-style theme: light dotted horizontal guide lines
theme_dot <- theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linetype = "dotted",
                                          colour = "grey60"),
        strip.background   = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
        legend.position    = "none")
```

## The source

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

In the first chapter, Cleveland uses a famous **barley experiment** to show how a good graph can expose a problem that numbers alone would never flag.

**The Data: **  Barley Yield (bushels per acre)

- 10 barley varieties
- 6 sites in Minnesota
- 2 years: **1931** and **1932**

<p style="font-size:0.6em; color:#93a1a1;">From *William S. Cleveland* *Visualizing Data* (1993),     
Hobart Press, Summit, New Jersey\br 
Original data: Immer, Hayes &amp; Powers (1934), *Journal of the American Society of Agronomy*, 26.</p>
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r preview}
barley |>
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarise(m = round(mean(yield), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = m) |>
  arrange(desc(site)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Site", "1931", "1932"), 
               label = " Average Yields in 6 sites")
```

<p style="font-size:0.6em; color:#93a1a1;"> 10 varieties × 6 sites × 2 years</p>
:::

::::


## Can you spot a problem? 
Original graphic: Yield by variety, by site for  2 years. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = variety)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9) +
  facet_grid(site ~ year) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linetype = "dotted",
                                          colour = "grey60"),
        strip.background   = element_rect(fill = "grey92"))
```

## Can you spot a problem? 
Revamped graphic: Yield by variety, by site for 2 years. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-align: center


ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = variety,  color = variety)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9 ) +
  facet_grid(site ~ year) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        )
```

## Grouping points
Maybe grouping varieties can help?

```{r dotplot-highligh, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8, fig.align="center"}

ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = site,  color = variety)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, size = 2.9,
             stroke = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Grouping points
Grouping varieties with some jitter

```{r dotplot-highlight-jitter, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8, fig.align="center"}

ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = site, color = variety)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1, size = 2.9, stroke = 1.1,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.2, seed = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r dotplot-highlight, fig.align="center", fig.height=4.8, fig.width=11}
#| eval: false
#| include: false

# Not run

ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = site)) +
  geom_point(data = filter(barley, !is_morris),
             shape = 1, size = 2.9, stroke = 1.1, colour = col_base) +
  geom_point(data = filter(barley, is_morris),
             shape = 1, size = 3.4, stroke = 1.6, colour = col_high) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", y = NULL) +
  theme_dot
```


## Cleveland 1993' Solution:  Multiway dot plot

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-align: center

# 1 = one column of 6 panels (as in the lattice/Trellis version); 2 = 2 columns
ncol_panels <- 1


ggplot(barley, aes(x = yield, y = variety, shape = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("1931" = 1, "1932" = 3), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ site, ncol = ncol_panels) +
  labs(x = "Barley yield (bushels per acre)", 
       y = NULL,
       caption = "At five sites, 1931 yields are higher than 1932. At Morris, it is the other way round") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linetype = "dotted",
                                          colour = "grey60"),
        strip.background   = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
        legend.position    = "bottom")
```


## Double lollipop: 1931 versus 1932

```{r double-lollipop, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.8, fig.align="center"}
site_means <- barley |>
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarise(m = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = m) |>
  mutate(is_morris = site == "Morris")

ggplot(site_means, aes(y = site)) +
  # Segments
  geom_segment(aes(x = `1931`, xend = `1932`, yend = site,
                   colour = is_morris), linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Dots
  geom_point(aes(x = `1931`, fill = "1931"),
             shape = 21, size = 4.6, stroke = 1.2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(x = `1932`, fill = "1932"),
             shape = 21, size = 4.6, stroke = 1.2, colour = "orange") +
  
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("1931" = "grey50", "1932" = "orange"),
                    name = NULL) +
  # Segment colors
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "grey20"),
                      guide = "none") +

  
  labs(x = "Mean barley yield for  6production sites (bushels per acre)",
       y = NULL, 
       title = "Visualizing the difference. 1931 -1932", 
       subtitle = "Double lolipop graphic", 
        caption = "At five sites, 1931 yields are higher than 1932. At Morris, it is the other way round") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

<p style="font-size:0.65em;">
Only in<strong>Morris</strong> did production go <strong>up</strong> from 1931 to  <span style="color:#E69F00;">1932</span>.
</p>

## Lollipop: change in mean yield, 1932 − 1931

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r lollipop, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
change <- barley |>
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarise(m = mean(yield), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = m) |>
  mutate(diff = `1932` - `1931`,
         is_morris = site == "Morris") |>
  arrange(diff) |>
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site))

ggplot(change, aes(x = diff, y = site, colour = is_morris)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = diff, yend = site), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = col_base, `TRUE` = col_high)) +
  labs(x = "Change in mean yield, 1932 − 1931 (bushels per acre)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        legend.position    = "none")
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
<div style="font-size:0.75em;">

- Five sites: yield **falls** in 1932
- **Morris**: yield **rises** by about 12 bushels per acre
- Morris moves in the opposite direction, and by a similar magnitude to the other sites' changes

</div>
:::

::::

## So what?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
<div style="font-size:0.8em;">

- Averages alone would hide this: Morris just looks like a site with a "good" 1932.
- The dot plots show that the **whole cloud of varieties** shifts at Morris, not just one or two outliers (in 1931, 9 of 10 varieties yield less at Morris than at the other sites on average; in 1932, all 10 yield more), which is unlikely to be chance.
- Cleveland's reading: the year labels for Morris were probably **swapped** in the data.
- A graph is a tool for **checking the data**, not only for presenting results.

</div>
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
<div style="font-size:0.75em;">

**Questions for discussion**

1. How would you confirm the suspected swap?
2. What would you do if the original records were lost?
3. Which other datasets in your work deserve this check?

</div>
:::

::::

Data source: vega-datasets / lattice `barley`. The conclusion about swapped years is Cleveland's interpretation; verify page references against your copy of the book.
